title: In-context Learning of Single-index Targets: Comparing Kernel and Feature Learners
authors: Haotian Gu, Yizhou Xu, Lenka Zdeborová
abstract: In-context learning (ICL) enables a pretrained model to infer a task from demonstrations without updating its parameters. While much of the existing theory focuses on linear target functions, in this paper we study nonlinear cases by comparing two one-layer attention architectures on the same family of single-index tasks. A kernel learner first maps inputs through a fixed nonlinear feature map and then applies linear attention, whereas a feature learner applies attention to the original input, followed by a learned nonlinear readout. We derive predictions for their memorization and generalization errors using the replica method, retaining the effects of pretraining size, task-pool diversity, and training and inference context lengths. The resulting predictions closely match numerical experiments across a broad range of regimes. Our analysis yields phase diagrams that characterize when each architecture is advantageous as the amount of pretraining data, task diversity, and context lengths vary. We further identify qualitatively different context-length scalings for the two learners. Together, these results clarify how architectural choices interact with the dataset and govern nonlinear in-context learning.
summary: This theoretical paper compares the performance of two attention-based architectures, the Kernel Learner and the Feature Learner, for performing nonlinear In-context Learning. Using advanced statistical physics techniques like the replica method, the authors derive phase diagrams that predict which architecture performs better based on system parameters. The work clarifies how architectural choices govern the ability of large models to learn tasks from limited demonstrations.
main_problem: The paper compares two distinct one-layer attention architectures, the Kernel Learner and the Feature Learner, for performing In-context Learning (ICL) on nonlinear single-index target tasks.
main_result: The analysis yields phase diagrams showing that the optimal architecture depends critically on the interplay between pretraining data size, task diversity, and context lengths, with the Feature Learner showing advantages in certain regimes.
method: The authors derive predictions for memorization and generalization errors using the replica method and establish asymptotic convergence results by analyzing the error bounds in the large-dimensional limits.
model_or_system: The model is ICL using pretrained Transformers to predict a label $y_0$ from demonstrations $\{(x_\ell, y_\ell)\}$. The comparison is between a Kernel Learner (fixed nonlinear feature map followed by linear attention) and a Feature Learner (attention on original input followed by learned nonlinear readout).
key_observables: Memorization Error ($E_M$) and Generalization Error ($E_G$) for both architectures.
important_parameters: Input dimension ($d$), feature dimension ($D$), pretraining size ($N$), task-pool size ($N_0$), and context lengths ($L, e_L$).
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on the replica method and assumes the task labels are generated by a noisy single-index model. Convergence proofs require specific moment bounds and continuity assumptions on the Gaussian channel.
figures_summary: Figure 1 schematically compares the two learners' architectures. Figure 2 compares Memorization and generalization errors vs. $N$ for the Feature, Linear attention, and Kernel learners.
paper_structure: The paper progresses from defining the problem and architectures, to deriving error predictions using the replica method, establishing asymptotic formulas for the errors, and finally proving the convergence of the feature-learner error to a limiting form.
why_interesting: The rigorous mathematical comparison of different learning architectures in the context of deep learning models (Transformers) provides theoretical insights into how model structure interacts with data statistics, which is highly relevant to understanding complex physical systems modeled by neural networks.

figures.caption: Figure 1: The kernel and feature learners. The kernel learner applies a fixed map h : Rd →RD before self-attention, whereas the feature learner applies a trainable readout bσ after self-attention.

Figure 2: Memorization (left) and generalization (right) errors as a function of N. We fix N0 = 24 and L = eL = 1024. Red, orange, and blue denote the feature learner, linear attention, and the kernel learner, respectively. Solid lines show replica predictions, and circles show numerical results from a single training run. The three learners use the same training and inference prompts.

Figure 3: Replica predictions for the relative errors of the two learners. In all panels, the color shows log2(Ekernel/Efeature). (a,b) Memorization and generalization as N/d2 and N0/d vary, with α = eα = 32; vertical dashed lines mark N = d2 and N = D2. (c,d) Memorization and generalization as the training length α = L/d and inference length eα = eL/d vary, with N0 = 24 and N = 12288; the diagonal dotted line marks equal lengths, and the horizontal dashed line marks eα = 32. Gold stars mark the shared parameter setting (N = 12288, N0 = 24, α = eα = 32). Blue favors the kernel learner, red favors the feature learner, and black curves indicate equal errors.
